title: Bom dia! — saying hello and introducing yourself
goal: Greet people by time of day, say your name and where you're from, and say thank you in the right form — while enjoying one big shortcut: Portuguese drops its subject pronouns, so "I" often disappears.
bekal: greet with *bom dia*, *boa tarde*, *boa noite* at the right time
use the six forms of the verb *ser* without looking at the table

dialogs.title: Diálogo — No aeroporto de Lisboa
dialogs.intro: Budi, an Indonesian student, has just landed in Lisbon. In the line at baggage claim he is standing next to Ana, a Portuguese student his age.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bom dia! Tudo bem, obrigado. E tu?
lines.id: Good morning! Fine, thanks. And you?
lines.literal: good day! all well, obliged(m). and you?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Estou bem, obrigada. Como te chamas?
lines.id: I'm fine, thanks. What's your name?
lines.literal: I-am(estar) well, obliged(f). how yourself you-call?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: My name is Budi. And you?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: I'm Ana. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Sou, sim. E tu, de onde és?
lines.id: Yes, I am. And you, where are you from?
lines.literal: I-am, yes. and you, from where you-are?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: How cool! Your Portuguese is good.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thanks, but I only speak a little.

notes: **Obrigado or obrigada?** This is the first mistake almost every beginner makes, and luckily also the easiest to fix. The form follows **the gender of the person saying thanks**, not the person being thanked. Budi is a man, so he always says *obrigado*; Ana is a woman, so she always says *obrigada*. Pick yours now and use it for life. (Literally it means "obliged".)

**Chamo-me, not me chamo.** The pronoun *me* goes **after** the verb, joined with a hyphen. This is one of the quickest giveaways that someone learned European Portuguese — in Brazil people say *me chamo Budi*. The full rule comes in Unit 12; for now, learn *chamo-me* as one solid block.

**Sou a Ana** — with *a* ("the") before her name. Portuguese puts an article in front of people's names, something English never does: *a Ana*, *o Pedro*, *o Budi*. In Portugal this is almost obligatory in everyday conversation. Leaving it out makes you sound like an official announcement.

**Sou indonésio, with no word for "I".** The form *sou* already contains "I", so *eu* doesn't need to be said. English can never drop its *I*; Portuguese drops it all the time. *Eu* appears only for emphasis or contrast: *Eu sou indonésio, ela é portuguesa* (I'm Indonesian, she's Portuguese).

**Sou, sim.** Portuguese often answers a question by repeating the verb, not with a bare *sim*. *És de Lisboa?* → *Sou.* It feels odd at first, but it's the most natural answer — a bit like English "I am". Adding *sim* after it adds emphasis: "yes, I am".

grammars.title: Ser — your first verb and the one you'll use most
body: *Ser* is one of the two Portuguese verbs for "to be". It's used for things that are **permanent**: who you are, where you're from, what you do. Its sibling, *estar*, is taken apart in Unit 3.
after: Notice that **one form serves three pronouns**: *é* is used for *ele*, *ela* and *você*. That's no accident — *você* was originally a polite third-person form (like "Your Grace"), which is why it never takes the *tu* form.
The pronoun itself is almost always dropped: *Sou professor*, not *Eu sou professor*. Coming from English, this is the first habit you have to let go of.

grammars.title: Tu, você, o senhor — choosing how to address someone
body: European Portuguese sorts the people you talk to much more carefully than English does — and more carefully than Brazilian Portuguese.

head: Address
Used for
Verb form
rows: friends, people your age, family, children
acquaintances you're not close to — **careful in Portugal**
older people, bosses, shop staff, formal situations

after: **An important warning that doesn't apply in Brazil:** in Portugal, *você* can sound **a little rude** to older people or strangers. The Portuguese often avoid it entirely and just use the third-person form with no pronoun at all: *Fala inglês?* ("Do you speak English?") — no *você*, no *o senhor*.
**A safe rule for beginners:** use *tu* with people your age whom you know, and *o senhor / a senhora* or a sentence with no pronoun for everyone else. You'll never go wrong this way.

blocks.text: Portuguese splits the day into three, and the boundaries aren't quite where English puts them — there's no separate greeting for "good afternoon" versus "good evening" at dusk.

head: Português
Say it
When to use it
English
rows: after dark — to say hello **and** goodbye
any time, very typical of Portugal

blocks.text: *Boa noite* does two jobs at once: it's your greeting when you walk into a restaurant at 8 p.m., and it's also your goodbye when you leave at 11. English splits these into "good evening" and "good night"; Portuguese doesn't.

head: Saying goodbye
Say it
English
Note

borrowed from Italian *ciao*, casual, very common

blocks.title: Don't throw adeus around
items: Language classes often teach *adeus* as a plain "goodbye". In Portugal it sounds like a real farewell — right for seeing someone off at the airport, not for walking out of a bakery.
For everyday use, say *até logo* or *tchau*. Both are safe almost anywhere.

blocks.text: **Não percebo** is a typically Portuguese phrase. In Brazil people say *não entendo*; both are correct and understood everywhere, but *perceber* is far more common in Lisbon. Learn this one — you'll use it constantly in your first week.

blocks.title: Portuguese words you already know
items: English took a handful of words straight from Portuguese: *a varanda* (veranda), *a marmelada* (marmalade — originally quince jam), *o flamingo*, *o albino*, *a cobra*. And thanks to Latin, thousands more are close cousins: *a família*, *o hospital*, *o hotel*, *o museu*, *a música*, *o problema*.
Most of them travel **without changing meaning**. The trick is to read them the Portuguese way: *hotel* is "oh-TEHL", *hospital* is "ohsh-pee-TAHL".
Make the most of this. Whenever a Portuguese word looks familiar, your guess is very likely right.
